emergencyRoutes.name: Call 999 or 112
emergencyRoutes.detail: Police, ambulance, fire or coastguard. 112 reaches exactly the same service. When you call from an iPhone, it tries to send your location to the emergency services automatically — you do not need an app to do that.

emergencyRoutes.name: Call 999 when you cannot speak
emergencyRoutes.detail: A silent 999 call does not automatically bring police. From a mobile, stay on the line and listen: an automated message will ask you to press 55. If you press 55, your call is put through to the police. If you don't, the call ends. Pressing 55 does not let the police find where you are. If you can, cough or tap the phone so they know someone is there.

emergencyRoutes.name: Text 999
emergencyRoutes.detail: Text 999 saying which service you need, what is happening and where you are. It is slower than a voice call, and a delivery report does not mean your message has been received.
emergencyRoutes.prerequisite: You must register your phone first. Text the word 'register' to 999 and reply 'yes' to the message you get back. This app cannot register you and cannot tell whether you are registered.

emergencyRoutes.name: 999 BSL
emergencyRoutes.detail: A free, 24-hour British Sign Language interpreter service for contacting 999.

emergencyRoutes.name: Relay UK — dial 18000
emergencyRoutes.detail: Dial 18000 to reach 999 through a relay assistant, if you are deaf, hard of hearing or have a speech impairment. 18000 is a number you call, not one you text.

services.name: National Domestic Abuse Helpline
services.summary: Free and confidential, 24 hours a day, for women experiencing domestic abuse and for anyone worried about someone. Run by Refuge. All the advisers are women.

services.name: Live Fear Free
services.summary: Wales's 24-hour helpline for anyone experiencing domestic abuse or sexual violence, and for anyone worried about someone. Calls are welcome in Welsh.
services.billingNote: Free from UK landlines and most mobile networks, and does not show on a phone bill. Some mobile networks may charge.

services.name: Scotland's Domestic Abuse and Forced Marriage Helpline
services.summary: Scotland's 24-hour helpline for anyone affected by domestic abuse or forced marriage, of any age or gender, and for anyone worried about someone.

services.name: Domestic and Sexual Abuse Helpline
services.summary: Northern Ireland's free, confidential 24-hour helpline for anyone affected by domestic or sexual abuse, and for anyone worried about someone.

services.name: 24/7 Rape and Sexual Abuse Support Line
services.summary: Free phone and online chat for anyone affected by rape, sexual assault or any sexual violence, whenever it happened. You can stay anonymous.

services.name: Rape Crisis Scotland Helpline
services.summary: Free, confidential support for people of any gender affected by sexual violence. Open every evening, 5pm until midnight.
services.billingNote: Calls do not show on a phone bill.

services.name: The Rowan Sexual Assault Referral Centre
services.summary: Northern Ireland's sexual assault referral centre, for children, young people, women and men, whether it happened recently or in the past. Answered at any hour.

services.name: Victim Support Supportline
services.summary: Free and confidential for anyone affected by crime. You can stay anonymous, you do not need to have told the police, and it does not matter how long ago it happened.

services.name: Victim Support Scotland
services.summary: Free support for anyone in Scotland affected by crime. You can talk through your options before deciding whether to tell the police.

services.name: Samaritans
services.summary: Someone to talk to, day or night, about anything that is troubling you, without judgement.
services.billingNote: Free from any phone, and the number won't come up on your phone bill.

services.name: Men's Advice Line
services.audience: Men, including trans and non-binary people
services.summary: Confidential support for men experiencing domestic abuse. Run by Respect. Not open at night or at weekends — outside those hours, Samaritans is open.
services.billingNote: Free, and calls will not appear on itemised bills.

services.name: Galop — LGBT+ abuse helpline
services.summary: For LGBT+ people experiencing domestic abuse, sexual violence, hate crime or conversion practices. Hours change during the week, so check before calling.

services.name: Women's Aid
services.summary: A directory of local domestic abuse services, a peer-support forum and the online Survivor's Handbook. Women's Aid has no phone line and its live chat has closed. For a helpline, call the National Domestic Abuse Helpline.

reporting.name: Report a crime
reporting.summary: Every way to report a crime, sent to the right police force for where you are — including Scotland, which is separate. Use it when nobody is in danger right now.

reporting.name: 101 — police, not an emergency
reporting.summary: For police matters when nobody is in danger and nothing is happening right now. It only works from within the UK. If you use a textphone, dial 18001 101.

reporting.name: Crimestoppers
reporting.summary: An independent charity, not the police. Tell them what you know about a crime completely anonymously — they do not take your name. Open at any hour.

reporting.name: British Transport Police
reporting.summary: For something on a train, the Tube or a tram that does not need an emergency response. You can text discreetly or call. If anyone is in danger, call 999 instead.
reporting.textNote: Texting may cost a small amount, and won't work if premium numbers are blocked or you have no credit.

reporting.name: StreetSafe
reporting.summary: Tell the police anonymously about a public place where you feel unsafe — a dark alleyway, somewhere you were followed. It is not for reporting a crime, and because it is anonymous nobody can come back to you.

guides.title: Emergency SOS
guides.summary: Calls the emergency services from your iPhone, even when it is locked. Pressing the side button five times only works if you turn on Call with 5 Presses first. Afterwards, it can text your emergency contacts your location.
steps: Settings > Emergency SOS: turn on Call with Hold and Release, Call with 5 Presses, or both.
Health app > tap your picture > Medical ID > Edit: add people you trust under Emergency Contacts.
guides.howToUse: Hold the side button and either volume button until the sliders appear and the countdown ends. Or, if you have turned on Call with 5 Presses, press the side button five times quickly. When the call ends, your emergency contacts get a text with your current location (if available), then updates for a while, unless you cancel. The text needs mobile service, and your contacts are not told if Messages is not your chosen messaging app (Settings > Apps > Default Apps > Messaging) or has been deleted.
guides.caution: By default, your iPhone plays a warning sound and counts down before it calls, and someone near you may hear it. After an emergency call, Do Not Disturb, Silence Unknown Callers and Screen Time may stop silencing calls for a while, so your phone may ring out loud if someone calls back. If SOS starts by accident, don't hang up: wait for the operator and explain that you don't need help. Bringing up the sliders also turns Face ID off until you next enter your passcode, which stops someone forcing you to unlock with your face, but keep holding and the SOS countdown starts. Only add emergency contacts you trust: they can be sent your location after any SOS call.
guides.requirements: Any iPhone. In the UK it calls 999 or 112.

guides.title: Medical ID and emergency contacts
guides.summary: Stores your medical details and who to contact, so first responders can see them from your Lock Screen. The people you add as emergency contacts are the ones Emergency SOS can text with your location.
steps: Health app > tap your picture > Medical ID > Get Started or Edit: fill in your details.
Under Emergency Contacts, tap Add Emergency Contact, choose the person, then add their relationship to you.
Scroll down and decide whether to turn on Show When Locked (read the caution first). The switch called Emergency Call or Share During Emergency Call has no effect in the UK.
guides.howToUse: If Show When Locked is on, someone can see your Medical ID by tapping Emergency on your Lock Screen passcode pad. Apple's automatic sharing during an emergency call is not available in the UK, so don't expect the 999 call handler to see it.
guides.caution: If you turn on Show When Locked, anyone holding your phone can read your medical details and see who your emergency contacts are, without your passcode. Don't turn it on if you're worried about someone who can get hold of your phone. Only add emergency contacts you trust: everyone listed can be sent your location after any Emergency SOS call. To remove someone quickly, Safety Check's Emergency Reset includes reviewing your emergency contacts.
guides.requirements: The Health app, on any iPhone.

guides.title: Check In
guides.summary: Lets someone you trust know when you arrive, or when a timer ends. If you don't respond, they are automatically sent the details you chose to share. You both need an iPhone with iOS 17 or later.
steps: Messages > open a conversation with the person > tap + > More > Check In > Edit.
Choose When I arrive or After a timer, set the details, then send.
To change how much it shares: Settings > Apps > Messages > Check In Data, then choose Limited or Full.
guides.howToUse: Your contact is alerted if you don't reach your destination, if you are significantly delayed and don't respond to the prompt to add time (you have 15 minutes), if the timer ends and you don't respond, or if you make an Emergency SOS call and don't respond to the follow-up prompt. They get a link showing what you chose to share: Limited (your location, battery and signal) or Full (also the route you've travelled and when you last unlocked your iPhone or took off your Apple Watch).
guides.caution: With a journey Check In, your contact learns your destination and roughly when you'll arrive as soon as you start. While it runs, your Lock Screen shows that a Check In is running. If your phone is lost, your contact is alerted as if you had not responded. If you lose signal or your iPhone switches off, they may be alerted late or early, so don't make Check In your only safeguard. Your contact needs an iPhone: someone with an Android phone can't receive it.
guides.requirements: iOS 17 or later, on your iPhone and on the other person's iPhone.

guides.title: Emergency SOS via satellite
guides.summary: Lets you text the emergency services when you have no mobile signal and no Wi-Fi, as long as you are outside with a clear view of the sky and the horizon.
steps: Update to the latest iOS, and set up your Medical ID and emergency contacts before you go somewhere with no signal.
Optional: go outside, then Settings > Emergency SOS > Try Demo, to practise. The demo does not call anyone.
guides.howToUse: Try calling 999 first. If the call can't connect, tap Emergency Text via Satellite and answer the questions on screen. Hold your iPhone naturally in your hand (you don't need to raise it) and follow the prompts to turn or move.
guides.caution: It only works when you have no mobile signal and no Wi-Fi, so it won't help somewhere with signal where you can't speak. Trees with light foliage can slow the connection; dense foliage, hills, canyons and tall structures can block it. A message may take 30 seconds to send, and over a minute under trees. Your location is shared with Apple and its relay providers. Telling your emergency contacts is optional. This is not the same as the UK's text-to-999 service.
guides.requirements: iPhone 14 or later. In the UK it needs iOS 16.2 or later. Apple says it is free for two years after your iPhone is activated.

guides.title: Crash Detection
guides.summary: If your iPhone detects a severe car crash and you don't respond, it calls the emergency services and texts your emergency contacts that you've been in a crash, with your location.
steps: It is on by default. Check that Settings > Emergency SOS > Call After Severe Crash is turned on.
To share your location with your emergency contacts: Settings > Privacy & Security > Location Services > System Services > turn on Emergency Calls & SOS.
guides.howToUse: After a severe crash, your iPhone shows an alert and counts down. Respond to the alert to cancel, or let the countdown finish and it calls the emergency services and plays them a recorded message. If a call is placed and you're fine, don't hang up: tell the operator you don't need help.
guides.caution: During the countdown your phone makes loud whoops, vibrates and flashes lights. The recorded message also plays out loud on your own phone, repeating every 5 seconds, so anyone near you will hear it. It shares your estimated latitude and longitude, with a search radius, even if Location Services is off. Your emergency contacts are not told if Messages is not your chosen messaging app or has been deleted. It cancels any other call you're on. Crash Detection cannot detect all car crashes.
guides.requirements: iPhone 14 or later with iOS 16 or later. Older iPhones don't have it, even when updated.

guides.title: Share My Location in Find My
guides.summary: Lets you share your live location with people you trust, and lets you check who you are sharing your location with in Find My.
steps: Find My > Me: turn on Share My Location. Location Services must be on.
To share with someone: Find My > People > + > Share My Location, add the person, send, then choose how long.
Check Find My > Me > Notifications About You, in case someone has set up alerts for when your location changes.
guides.howToUse: To check who can see you, open Find My > People and tap each name to see whether you are sharing with them. People also lists people who share with you, and Family Sharing members appear there automatically. To stop, tap their name > Stop Sharing My Location, or turn off Share My Location under Me.
guides.caution: When you stop sharing, the other person may notice, and on older software they may get a notification in Messages, so this is not a silent way to cut someone off. People you share with see you in Find My, Messages, Maps and Contacts, and may see which direction and how fast you're travelling. Anyone who knows your Apple Account password can see your devices in Find My > Devices: check that list and remove any device you don't recognise. Find My can locate your iPhone for up to 24 hours after it is turned off. You can turn off iPhone Findable After Power Off on the power-off screen, but then you can't find a lost phone. If someone uses Precision Finding to find you, you get a notification. Find My can't be turned off while Stolen Device Protection is on.
guides.requirements: Any iPhone signed in to your Apple Account, with Location Services on for Find My.

guides.title: Show Previews
guides.summary: Controls whether the text of a message or email, or the details of a calendar invitation, appear on your Lock Screen, where anyone glancing at your phone could read them.
steps: Settings > Notifications > Show Previews.
Choose Always, When Unlocked or Never.
To change one app only: Settings > Notifications > [the app].
guides.howToUse: Set it to Never if you don't want message and email text or calendar invitation details on a Lock Screen someone else might see.
guides.caution: The notification itself still appears on the Lock Screen; only the preview is hidden. To keep an app off the Lock Screen completely, go to Settings > Notifications > [the app] and, under Alerts, turn off Lock Screen. Not all apps support previews, so check the ones that matter to you. Notifications show while you share your screen unless you turn them off at Settings > Notifications > Screen Sharing.

guides.title: Lock or hide an app
guides.summary: Makes an app need Face ID, Touch ID or your passcode to open, and can move it off your Home Screen into a hidden folder.
steps: Touch and hold the app on the Home Screen until the quick actions menu opens.
Tap Require Face ID. Then tap Require Face ID again to lock the app, or tap Hide and Require Face ID, authenticate, and tap Hide App to lock and hide it.
guides.howToUse: To open a hidden app, swipe to App Library, tap the Hidden folder, then use Face ID, Touch ID or your passcode. A locked app's content is kept out of notification previews, search, Siri suggestions and call history.
guides.caution: This does not fully conceal an app. The Hidden folder still shows in App Library, and hidden app names can appear in Settings > Apps > Hidden Apps, in Screen Time, in Battery > Battery Health & Charging, and in your App Store purchase history. Calculator, Camera, Clock, Contacts, Find My, Maps, Shortcuts and Settings can't be locked. Your ordinary passcode opens a locked app, so someone who knows it can still get in, unless Stolen Device Protection is on and you're away from a familiar location. In Family Sharing, a parent or guardian can see that a 13 to 17-year-old downloaded an app and how long they use it.
guides.requirements: Only apps you download from the App Store can be hidden; built-in apps, and the app you use as your default browser, can't be. Locking and hiding are set on each device and don't sync through iCloud.

guides.title: Stolen Device Protection
guides.summary: Adds a Face ID or Touch ID check, with no passcode fallback, for sensitive actions when your iPhone is away from places it knows, such as home or work.
steps: Settings > Face ID & Passcode (Touch ID & Passcode on an iPhone with a Home button), enter your passcode > Stolen Device Protection: turn it on.
For stronger protection: on the same screen, Require Security Delay > Always.
guides.howToUse: Nothing to do day to day. Away from familiar locations, sensitive actions need Face ID or Touch ID with no passcode fallback, and critical changes to your account also need a one-hour delay.
guides.caution: Home counts as a familiar location, so by default it does not stop someone at home who knows your passcode. Only Require Security Delay set to Always closes that gap. But Always slows you down too: changing your own passcode or Apple Account password always needs a one-hour wait, even at home, which delays locking out someone who has learned your passcode. The check accepts any face or fingerprint set up on the phone, so if someone may have added their own Face ID appearance, reset Face ID first. Turning it on needs Significant Locations, Apple's location history. While it is on, Find My can't be turned off, so your devices stay findable by anyone with your Apple Account password. Changing your Apple Account password on the iPhone can briefly hide your devices' location on iCloud.com.
guides.requirements: iOS 17.3 or later, with two-factor authentication, a passcode, Face ID or Touch ID, Significant Locations and Find My all turned on.

guides.title: Sensitive Content Warning
guides.summary: Blurs photos and videos that may contain nudity before you see them, in Messages, AirDrop, FaceTime, shared photo albums and Contact Posters, and offers ways to get help or block the sender.
steps: Settings > Privacy & Security > Sensitive Content Warning: turn it on.
On the same screen, check which apps it covers.
guides.howToUse: When a blurred image arrives with a warning, you can choose to view it, get safety resources or block the sender. If it came in an iMessage or a FaceTime video call, you can report the sender to Apple: the content is then sent to Apple, which may pass it to the police.
guides.caution: Detection happens on your iPhone and is approximate, so some images may not be caught. The warning itself creates no record with Apple. It only blurs images already sent to you; it doesn't stop someone sending them. It also warns you before you send such images, and turning it on turns it on for a paired Apple Watch too.
guides.requirements: iOS 17 or later. For adults it is off until you turn it on.

guides.title: Unwanted tracking notifications
guides.summary: Warns you if an AirTag, AirPods, another Find My accessory or a compatible Bluetooth tracker that isn't yours seems to be moving with you over time.
steps: Settings > Privacy & Security > Location Services: turn it on, then System Services > Find My iPhone: on.
Settings > Bluetooth: on. Make sure Airplane Mode is off.
Settings > Notifications > Tracking Notifications: turn on Allow Notifications.
guides.howToUse: If you get an alert, tap it, then tap Play Sound, or Find Nearby to use Precision Finding. You can find it again later in Find My > Items > Items Detected With You (your iPhone may call it Unknown Items Detected with You). Check places you rarely look, such as a jacket pocket, the outer compartment of a bag, or your car.
guides.caution: Before you change anything, including disabling the item, think about how that could affect your safety. Disabling it stops its owner getting its location, which the owner may notice, and stops your alerts for it. First take a screenshot of the item and owner details, and keep the item: the police may need it and its serial number. Holding your iPhone near the item shows the last four digits of the owner's phone number. Turning off Bluetooth, Location Services or Find My on your own iPhone does not stop the owner tracking the item. If you can't find it and feel unsafe, go to a safe public place and contact the police. Alerts are not guaranteed: an item that was with you overnight may not be flagged.
guides.requirements: iOS 14.5 or later for AirTags and Find My accessories; iOS 17.5 or later for other Bluetooth trackers that follow the cross-platform standard.

guides.title: Safety Check
guides.summary: A screen in Settings to see which people and apps can access your information, and to stop sharing with them one by one or all at once if you feel unsafe. It has a Quick Exit button.
steps: Make sure you are signed in to your Apple Account on the iPhone, with two-factor authentication on.
Settings > Privacy & Security > Safety Check.
Choose Emergency Reset to stop all sharing at once, or Manage Sharing & Access to review person by person.
guides.howToUse: Tap Emergency Reset, then Start Emergency Reset, and follow the prompts to stop sharing with every person and app Safety Check covers, review your devices and emergency contacts, and change your passcode and Apple Account password. Tap Quick Exit at any time to close Settings straight away; changes you made before that are kept.
guides.caution: Apple says to think about the impact on your safety and privacy before you make changes. Changes to sharing or access may be noticed by others, so plan for the other person finding out. Cutting off sharing can also cut you off from tools and information you rely on. Safety Check can't reach non-Apple accounts, social media, or devices signed in to a different Apple Account. If someone else controls Screen Time on your iPhone, or it has a management profile, some options may not be available. If you start sharing again later, some apps or services send a notification about it.
guides.requirements: iOS 16 or later. It works differently if Stolen Device Protection is also on.

rights.title: What counts as domestic abuse
rights.summary: Domestic abuse is not only hitting. It includes controlling you, cutting you off from people, threats, sexual abuse and controlling your money. Much of it is a crime, and the law still protects you after you split up.

points.text: The legal definition covers physical, sexual, emotional and economic abuse, and controlling or coercive behaviour, by a partner, ex-partner or relative. Both of you must be 16 or over.
Controlling or coercive behaviour is a crime, including by an ex-partner or relative. It can lead to up to 5 years in prison.
Scotland has its own crime of abusing a partner or ex-partner. It covers controlling, isolating, monitoring, frightening or humiliating you, not just violence.
Northern Ireland has a domestic abuse offence covering partners, ex-partners and close family members. It needs abusive behaviour on two or more occasions.
Economic or financial abuse counts as domestic abuse. That includes controlling your money, holding money back or stopping you from working.

rights.whatYouCanDo: If you are in danger now, call 999. Otherwise you can report it to the police on 101, or talk in confidence to the domestic abuse helpline for your nation.
rights.nationDifferences: Scotland's offence covers partners and ex-partners. The offences in England and Wales and in Northern Ireland also cover family members. Northern Ireland's offence needs abuse on two or more occasions. In England and Wales, the abuser must repeatedly or continuously behave in a controlling or coercive way that has a serious effect on you.

rights.title: Ask police about a partner
rights.summary: You can ask the police whether your partner or an ex-partner has a history of abuse. A friend or relative can ask for you. The police decide what to share and who to tell, and you will be asked to agree to keep it confidential.

points.text: In England and Wales this is the Domestic Violence Disclosure Scheme, also called "Clare's Law". You can ask about a partner or ex-partner. Police should finish a check within 28 days, unless there are good reasons it takes longer.
In Scotland it is the Disclosure Scheme for Domestic Abuse Scotland. If you ask about someone else's partner, police tell the person at risk, not you.
In Northern Ireland the scheme is called DVADS. You must be 16 or over to apply, and it covers partners and ex-partners.
Police can also share information to protect someone at risk without being asked. This is called the "right to know" in England and Wales, and "Power to Tell" in Scotland.

rights.whatYouCanDo: Apply online, phone the police on 101, or go to a police station. If the police tell you they have nothing to share, it does not mean the person is safe. If you are in danger now, call 999.
rights.nationDifferences: The schemes have different names: Clare's Law in England and Wales, DSDAS in Scotland and DVADS in Northern Ireland. If you apply about someone else, the information usually goes to the person at risk. In England and Wales you may simply be told there is no information to disclose to you, even if the person at risk was told something.

rights.title: Court orders to keep you safe
rights.summary: A court can order an abuser to stop harming or threatening you, or to stay away from your home. In England and Wales, the police can also give an abuser a notice banning them from your home.

points.text: You can apply for a non-molestation order, or an occupation order that decides who can live in the family home. There's no fee to apply, and breaking a non-molestation order is a crime.
If a senior police officer believes someone aged 18 or over has been violent or threatened violence towards you, they can give that person a notice that can ban them from your home.

Domestic abuse protection orders are being piloted. You can only apply for one if the abuser lives in Greater Manchester, Croydon, Bromley, Sutton, Hartlepool, Middlesbrough, Redcar and Cleveland, Stockton-on-Tees or North Wales. Applying is free. The pilot is due to end on 24 November 2026.
You can ask a court for an interdict, an exclusion order or a non-harassment order. Breaking a domestic abuse interdict with a power of arrest attached is a crime.
There is no court fee for a non-molestation or occupation order, but you may have to pay to have the papers served. Breaking a non-molestation order is a crime.

rights.whatYouCanDo: Talk to a solicitor or a domestic abuse charity. In England and Wales, if you apply for legal aid for a protection order, the usual upper income and savings limits are waived, though you may have to pay a contribution.
rights.nationDifferences: Police notices and domestic abuse protection orders are for England and Wales only.

rights.title: Housing help if you leave
rights.summary: If abuse means you can't stay at home, you can get help with housing. Ask your council, or the Housing Executive in Northern Ireland. In England and Wales, being homeless because of domestic abuse gives you "priority need", if you are eligible for help.

points.text: If you are homeless because of domestic abuse, you are automatically in "priority need". If you are eligible for help, the council must find you somewhere to stay while it looks into your case, and it may then have to house you. It cannot pass your case to a council in an area where you would be at risk of abuse.
If you have no recourse to public funds, you are not usually eligible for this help. Get advice from a domestic abuse service first, and ask about the Destitute Domestic Violence Concession.
If you are homeless because of domestic abuse, Welsh housing law also puts you in priority need.
Your council has a legal duty to help you if you're homeless, and must provide temporary accommodation if you need it. You count as homeless if staying in your home would probably lead to abuse.
Go to the Housing Executive, not the council. It will assess your needs and may give you temporary accommodation while it helps you find a permanent home.

rights.whatYouCanDo: Contact your council's homelessness team. In Northern Ireland, contact the Housing Executive on 03448 920 900, or 03448 920 908 out of hours.
rights.nationDifferences: England and Wales give people made homeless by domestic abuse "priority need". Scotland counts you as homeless if staying at home would probably lead to abuse. In Northern Ireland, the Housing Executive deals with homelessness.

sources.title: Homelessness code of guidance for local authorities - Chapter 21: Domestic abuse - Guidance - GOV.UK
If you're homeless or have nowhere safe to stay - mygov.scot
Domestic Abuse Support - Northern Ireland Housing Executive

rights.title: Sexual violence and consent
rights.summary: Sex or sexual touching without your consent is a crime. You can get help from a sexual assault referral centre without going to the police first. You can report rape or sexual assault at any time, even years later.

points.text: In law, you consent only if you agree by choice and have the freedom and capacity to make that choice.
You can change your mind at any time, even during sex. Agreeing to one thing does not mean you agree to everything.
There is no time limit for reporting rape or sexual assault to the police.
If you report a sexual offence, nothing that identifies you may be published in your lifetime.
You can go to a sexual assault referral centre for care without reporting to the police first.

rights.whatYouCanDo: If you are in danger, call 999. Contact a sexual assault referral centre for care, even if you haven't decided about the police. Go as soon as you can.
rights.nationDifferences: In Scotland, forensic samples can be kept for 26 months, so you can decide to report later. In Northern Ireland, nothing that identifies a victim of a sexual offence may be published in their lifetime or for 25 years after their death, and suspects who are not charged also have anonymity.

rights.title: Stalking and harassment
rights.summary: Stalking is a pattern of unwanted behaviour that makes you scared or distressed. It can mean following you, contacting you again and again, or watching you online. It is a crime everywhere in the UK, and courts can order a stalker to stay away.

points.text: Stalking is a crime. It can include following you, repeatedly contacting you, spying on you, or monitoring your phone, email or internet use.
Courts can make a stalking protection order or a restraining order to stop a stalker's behaviour.

Report early. The less serious charges must be brought within 6 months of the last incident. The more serious charges, where you feared violence or it seriously affected your daily life, have no 6-month limit.
If someone is convicted of stalking you on or after 1 September 2026, the court must make a non-harassment order to protect you, unless it decides you don't need one.
Police can apply for a stalking protection order lasting 2 to 5 years. Breaking it can mean up to 5 years in prison.

rights.whatYouCanDo: Keep a diary and save messages, emails, call logs, letters and gifts as evidence. Don't reply to them or agree to meet. Report it to the police: 999 if you are in danger, otherwise 101.
rights.nationDifferences: In Scotland, courts protect you with non-harassment orders. Northern Ireland and England and Wales have stalking protection orders.

rights.title: Intimate images and online abuse
rights.summary: Sharing or threatening to share intimate images of you without consent is a crime. In England and Wales, making a sexual deepfake of you is now a crime too. Online platforms must have systems to remove intimate images you report, within 48 hours at most.

points.text: Sharing, or threatening to share, an intimate photo or video of you without your consent is a crime in every UK nation. The exact rules differ.
A threat to share is a crime even if the photo doesn't exist, or if it is fake.
Since 6 February 2026, it is a crime to create a sexual deepfake of an adult without consent, or to ask someone to make one.
Sending someone an unwanted sexual image, such as a photo of genitals ("cyberflashing"), is a crime.

Since 29 June 2026, online platforms must have systems to remove an intimate image shared without consent as soon as they can, and within 48 hours at most, after the person shown (or someone acting for them) reports it. A platform can refuse if it decides the image is not covered.

rights.whatYouCanDo: Keep evidence (screenshots, links, usernames), then report it to the platform and the police as soon as you can: in England and Wales, some of these charges have time limits.
rights.nationDifferences: In England and Wales, the basic sharing offence must be charged within 6 months, and making a deepfake within 3 years; the more serious sharing offences and threats have no 6-month limit. The basic offence there needs no intent to cause distress. In Scotland it is a crime if the person meant to cause fear, alarm or distress, or was reckless about it. In Northern Ireland it is a crime if they meant to cause distress.

sources.title: Abusive Behaviour and Sexual Harm (Scotland) Act 2016

rights.title: Your rights at work
rights.summary: The law protects you from unfair treatment at work because you are pregnant. Women and men must get equal pay for equal work. In England, Scotland and Wales, your employer must take steps to prevent sexual harassment.

points.text: Your employer must not treat you unfairly, discriminate against you or dismiss you because you are pregnant. Pregnant employees get paid time off for antenatal care.
Men and women must get equal pay for doing equal work.
Your employer must take steps to prevent sexual harassment at work. Since 6 April 2026, reporting sexual harassment can count as whistleblowing, which the law protects.
Act fast: for most claims, you must contact Acas within 3 months minus 1 day. This changes to 6 months minus 1 day where your time limit starts on or after 1 October 2026.
Northern Ireland has its own law against sex discrimination and harassment at work. Tribunal claims usually must be made within 3 months, or 6 months for unequal pay.

rights.whatYouCanDo: Raise it with your employer, in writing if you can, and keep notes and evidence. Get advice from Acas (England, Scotland, Wales) or the Labour Relations Agency (Northern Ireland: 03300 555 300).
rights.nationDifferences: In Northern Ireland, claims go to an Industrial Tribunal, and sacking a woman because she is pregnant is sex discrimination.

rights.title: Your rights as a victim
rights.summary: If a crime happens to you, you have rights. They include help to understand and be understood, support, updates on your case and, in many cases, a chance to tell the court how the crime has affected you.

points.text: The Victims' Code gives you 12 rights. Some, such as being referred to support services, apply even if you don't report the crime to the police.
You have the right to an interpreter when reporting, being interviewed or giving evidence, and to be told about important decisions in your case.
You can make a Victim Personal Statement telling the court how the crime affected you. You can say whether you'd like to read it aloud or have it read for you, but the judge or magistrate decides.
The Victims' Code for Scotland sets out your rights, including to information about your case and to understand and be understood. You can ask for a decision not to prosecute to be reviewed.
The Victim Charter gives you free interpretation, information about your case, and a written statement to the court on how the crime affected you. You are not entitled to read it aloud in court.

rights.whatYouCanDo: Ask the police which rights apply to you, and ask for a copy of the Victims' Code or Victim Charter. If your rights are not met, you can complain to the organisation involved.
rights.nationDifferences: In Northern Ireland, you make a Victim Personal Statement through Victim Support NI, the NSPCC Young Witness Service (for young people) or a PSNI family liaison officer. In England and Wales, the rights to understand and be understood, to be referred to support, and to complain apply to all victims.

rights.title: Forced marriage and FGM
rights.summary: Nobody can force you to marry. Forced marriage and female genital mutilation (FGM) are crimes across the UK. Courts can make orders to protect you, and the Forced Marriage Unit can help, including if you are abroad.

points.text: Forcing someone to marry is a crime, and that includes religious ceremonies that are not legally binding.
If you're under 18, any marriage counts as a forced marriage, even without pressure. Arranging a marriage for someone before they turn 18 is a crime.
A court can make a forced marriage protection order, for example ordering someone to hand over your passport. In an emergency, an order can be made straight away.
FGM is a crime, and so is taking a girl or woman who is a UK national, or who normally lives in the UK, abroad for FGM. The maximum sentence is 14 years in prison.
You can apply to a court for an FGM protection order to keep you or someone you know safe. In England and Wales it is free, and you don't have to reveal your identity.

rights.whatYouCanDo: If you are in danger, call 999. The Forced Marriage Unit: 020 7008 0151 (Monday to Friday, 9am to 5pm), 020 7008 5000 out of hours, or fmu@fcdo.gov.uk. NSPCC FGM helpline: 0800 028 3550.
rights.nationDifferences: In Scotland, people under 16 cannot consent to marriage, and courts can also make forced marriage protection orders. In Northern Ireland, you apply for an FGM protection order to the High Court or a county court.

rights.title: Harassment in public places
rights.summary: Being threatened, harassed or intimidated in public is against the law. In England and Wales, harassing someone because of their sex is now a separate crime with a longer maximum prison sentence.

points.text: Since 1 April 2026, it is a separate crime to deliberately harass, alarm or distress someone because of their sex. It can mean up to 2 years in prison.

The government says it can cover things like obscene comments, threats of sexual violence and threatening invasions of personal space, in streets, parks, public transport, taxis and shops, when they are done on purpose to harass, alarm or distress you because of your sex.
Threatening or abusive behaviour likely to make a reasonable person afraid or alarmed is a crime. So are unwanted sexual comments meant to upset you or for sexual thrills.
Threatening or abusive behaviour likely to make a reasonable person afraid or alarmed is a crime, even if it happens once. It can mean up to 5 years in prison.

rights.whatYouCanDo: If you feel unsafe, go somewhere busy and call 999. Afterwards, write down the time, place and what happened, and report it to the police on 101.
rights.nationDifferences: The offence of harassing someone because of their sex applies in England and Wales. Scotland will add sex to its hate crime law from 5 April 2027, but that is not in force yet. In Scotland and Northern Ireland, the general offences of threatening or abusive behaviour apply.

refuges.name: National Domestic Abuse Helpline
refuges.summary: Free, 24 hours a day, every day. Advisers can help you find a refuge vacancy for you and your children, or other specialist services near you. Confidential, in many languages, with BSL video relay on weekdays from 10am to 6pm.

refuges.name: Women's Aid Directory
refuges.summary: Search by area for local, regional and national domestic abuse and refuge services, including specialist services for Black and minoritised, d/Deaf and disabled, and LGBT+ survivors, and contact them directly.

refuges.name: Your local council
refuges.summary: If you're homeless because of domestic abuse and eligible for help, you automatically have priority need for accommodation. The council should give you somewhere to stay straight away while it looks into your case, and should not insist on police evidence. You can apply to any council, and it cannot pass your case to one in an area where you would be at risk of abuse. Women with no recourse to public funds are not usually eligible: a local domestic abuse service can apply to Southall Black Sisters' No Recourse Fund for you.

refuges.name: Southall Black Sisters
refuges.audience: Casework is for women living in Ealing, Hounslow or Hillingdon. The helpline is open to women elsewhere.
refuges.summary: Specialist domestic abuse support, delivered by and for Black and minoritised women. Its No Recourse Fund helps migrant women across the UK with no recourse to public funds pay for safe accommodation and living costs; your local domestic abuse service applies for you. The helpline is not open 24 hours, and you may need to leave a voicemail. For an urgent refuge space, it directs you to the National Domestic Abuse Helpline.

refuges.name: Live Fear Free Helpline
refuges.summary: 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Advisers can put you in touch with safe emergency accommodation through a national network of refuges, as well as other support.

refuges.name: Find your local service (Welsh Women's Aid)
refuges.summary: Lists specialist domestic abuse and sexual violence services by local authority area across Wales. The Welsh Government says you can get a refuge place through the Live Fear Free Helpline or your local group.

refuges.name: Your local council
refuges.summary: If you're homeless because of domestic abuse, Welsh law puts you in priority need. Your council must assess your case, and should give you emergency accommodation while it does.

refuges.name: Bawso
refuges.audience: Black, minority ethnic and migrant survivors
refuges.summary: Free, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Wales's lead specialist service for survivors from ethnic minorities, offering safe accommodation in refuges and safe houses as well as crisis support. It takes referrals from all over the UK.

refuges.name: Scotland's Domestic Abuse and Forced Marriage Helpline
refuges.summary: 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Managed by Scottish Women's Aid. It can direct you to your local Women's Aid group, Scotland's only refuge providers. To get a refuge place you contact that group, which checks space and suitability. If no refuge is free, the group can help you get temporary accommodation from your council.

refuges.name: Find your nearest Women's Aid group
refuges.summary: Search for your local Women's Aid group, with phone numbers and, for most groups, email and office hours, and contact it about a refuge place. Most groups are open on weekdays in office hours only. Out of hours, call the helpline or contact your council.

refuges.name: Your local council
refuges.summary: Your local council has a legal duty to help you if you're homeless, and must provide temporary accommodation if you need it. If you leave because of domestic abuse, you might stay with friends or family, in a refuge, or in temporary accommodation the council provides.

refuges.name: Domestic and Sexual Abuse Helpline
refuges.summary: Free and confidential, 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. Operators talk through your options and can support you to make a referral to refuge or emergency accommodation. Local Women's Aid groups keep office hours, so out of hours this is the way into refuge. Managed and delivered by Nexus.

refuges.name: Local Women's Aid groups
refuges.summary: There are 12 Women's Aid refuges across Northern Ireland, run by the local groups. Find your local group and contact it directly to ask about a space. Groups are open Monday to Friday, 9am to 5pm; out of hours, call the Domestic and Sexual Abuse Helpline.

refuges.name: Northern Ireland Housing Executive
refuges.summary: Homelessness help in Northern Ireland comes from the Housing Executive, not the council. It will assess your housing needs, and may give you temporary accommodation while it helps you find a permanent home. Out of hours (5pm to 9am on weekdays, and at weekends and on public holidays), call 03448 920 908.

refugeNote.text: Kitty G never shows where a refuge is. Refuge addresses are kept confidential to keep the women and children living there safe, as Women's Aid in England, Scotland's national helpline and the Welsh Government all say. These are the services that can help you find a place.
